701.quote_or_event: “A monk who, on receiving an order from his superior, walks up to him, watching his nods and motions, is called well-behaved.”
701.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana opens its lecture on discipline by defining the good disciple as one who attends to his teacher's unspoken nods and gestures, not only to his words.
701.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats reading a superior's silent signs as the mark of the person most worth having in the presence of authority.
701.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
701._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Close fit on reading a superior's gestures; the setting is pupil and teacher rather than minister and king.

702.quote_or_event: “He reached the knowledge called Manaḥparyāya, by which he knew the thoughts of all sentient beings, with five organs, which are not defective, and possess a developed intellect, (living) in the two and a half continents and the two oceans.”
702.explanation: When Mahavira took up the ascetic life he gained manaḥparyāya jñāna, the direct knowledge of other beings' minds, which Jainism counts among the higher, supersensory kinds of knowledge.
702.tie_back: The Kural sets the one who knows another's mind without doubt beside the divine; Jain scripture likewise treats certain knowledge of other minds as a mark of the most advanced souls.
702.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.15.23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)
702._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on wisdomlib.org. Good thematic fit on mind-reading as a near-divine power. In Jainism, though, it is a spiritual faculty that comes from destroying karma, not worldly shrewdness, and Jainism has no creator god to compare it to.

703.quote_or_event: “An intelligent man who has learned (the sacred texts) takes his duties upon himself, and he becomes renowned in the world; as the earth is the dwelling of all beings, so he will be a dwelling of all duties.”
703.explanation: The verse follows the praise of the pupil who guesses his teacher's thoughts and needs no express directions (1.43–44), and calls such a person a support on which everything rests.
703.tie_back: The Kural says such perceptive people should be won at any price, and the Jain text says the same kind of person becomes indispensable, a 'dwelling of all duties'.
703.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.45 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
703._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. This is a partial match: it praises the perceptive disciple's worth, but says nothing about paying any price to secure such helpers.

704.quote_or_event: “An excellent pupil needs no express directions, or he is (at least) quickly directed; he always carries out his duties as he is told.”
704.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana sets the pupil who understands without being told against the 'ill-behaved' one who stays insubordinate and inattentive even when given an order (1.3).
704.tie_back: Both texts divide people who look alike into two different kinds: those who grasp what is wanted without being told, and those who do not.
704.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.44 (cf. 1.2–3) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
704._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on understanding without being told; the Kural's 'alike in body' contrast is only implied by the Jain pairing of good and bad pupils.

705.quote_or_event: “He should not, in every case, wait for the express command (of the teacher) like an unbroken horse for the whip (of the rider), but like a broken horse which sees the whip (of the rider) he should commit no evil act.”
705.explanation: The trained horse responds to the sight of the whip and does not need the blow; the good disciple likewise acts on what he sees rather than waiting to be told outright.
705.tie_back: The verse turns on the eye's job of reading a sign, which is the faculty the Kural says is worthless if it cannot read intentions.
705.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
705._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Partial match: it praises perceiving from a visible sign, but does not make the Kural's rhetorical point about the eye being useless otherwise.

706.quote_or_event: “The alteration produced on the soul, just as on a crystal by the presence of black things, &c., is denoted by the word lêsyâ.”
706.explanation: In Jacobi's note to the lecture on leśyās he quotes this verse from the Avacūri commentary. It explains the soul's 'colourings' (black through white) as reflections of the karma that accompanies it, the way a clear crystal takes on the colour of what lies beside it.
706.tie_back: Jainism uses the same crystal image as the Kural: just as the crystal shows its neighbour's colour, the soul shows the colour of the dispositions that dominate it.
706.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 34, note 1 by Jacobi quoting the Avacūri commentary (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
706._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi's footnote on sacred-texts.com. The crystal simile matches almost exactly, but it comes from a commentary verse quoted in a note, not from the sutra text, and it is about the soul taking colour from karma rather than the face showing the heart.

707.quote_or_event: “Perceiving the teacher's anger one should pacify him by kindness, appease him with folded hands, and promise not to do wrong again.”
707.explanation: The disciple is expected to notice his teacher's anger as soon as it shows and respond to it at once with humility.
707.tie_back: It assumes what the Kural states: anger shows itself before anything is said, so the attentive person can read it.
707.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.41 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
707._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: the Jain verse is about responding to visible anger, not about the face as the first herald of pleasure and anger.

708.quote_or_event: “Guessing the teacher's thoughts and the purport of his words, one should express one's assent, and execute (what he desires to be done).”
708.explanation: The ideal disciple reads his teacher's thoughts and acts on them, so the teacher does not have to explain what he needs.
708.tie_back: The Kural says it is enough to stand before those who read the heart; the Jain verse describes exactly that kind of attendant from the other side.
708.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.43 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
708._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on grasping another's need without being told; the Kural's specific case of someone in trouble showing only their face is not in the verse.

709.quote_or_event: Hemacandra tells how the serpent Caṇḍakauśika, reborn as a snake whose very look was poisonous because of anger carried over from former lives, turned its deadly glare on the wandering Mahavira. Mahavira's calm, unhostile gaze did not change, and the serpent was pacified and awakened.
709.explanation: The episode sets the look of hatred against the look of compassion and shows that anger carried in the soul comes out through the eyes.
709.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's claim that the eyes declare enmity or friendship to anyone who can read them.
709.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10 (Mahāvīra-caritra), ch. 3, part 10, 'Episode of Caṇḍakauśika' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)
709._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from the episode as summarised on wisdomlib.org; not quoted. The eye's power to show hostility or goodwill is present, but the story is about overcoming anger, not about a reader of glances judging friend and foe.

710.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra classes knowledge gained through the senses and mind (mati) and through testimony (śruta) as parokṣa, indirect, and keeps the name pratyakṣa, direct, for knowledge the soul has without the senses: clairvoyance, knowledge of other minds, and omniscience.
710.explanation: For Jainism, any judgment that relies on the eye is a mediated and limited instrument. Only the purified soul knows another being directly.
710.tie_back: The Kural says the eye is the only measuring rod even the subtle have, while Jainism agrees that ordinary judges rely on the senses but holds that a higher, eye-free knowing exists.
710.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 1.11–12 (cf. tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)
710._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known doctrine, not quoted. This is a next-best match: Jainism partly disagrees with the Kural by placing direct, non-sensory knowledge above any reading of the eyes.
